title: Snapshot Isolation Update Conflict (Error 3960)
description: SNAPSHOT isolation aborts a read-modify-write with error 3960 when another session changed the row; serialize it or reserve the row with UPDLOCK. Why it matters: optimistic concurrency (SNAPSHOT isolation) trades blocking for outright transaction failures under contention -- a tradeoff every team adopting it needs to understand before they hit it in production.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Imagine two editors both open the same shared document at the same moment, each one reading the current text, thinking about a change, and then saving their own edit back. If the document-editing system is smart enough to notice "wait, someone else already changed this since you opened it," it can refuse the second save and tell that editor "go look again, things changed underneath you" — rather than silently letting the second save blindly overwrite the first editor's change without either of them ever knowing a conflict happened. This lesson is about SQL Server's SNAPSHOT isolation level doing exactly that kind of conflict detection, and about the specific error it raises when it catches this happening.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** SNAPSHOT isolation is a way of achieving isolation using row versioning instead of locking — a reader under SNAPSHOT isolation sees a consistent picture of the data as it existed at the moment its transaction started, without taking locks that would block writers, and without being blocked by other writers' locks either. This is often called "optimistic concurrency" — instead of locking things up front to prevent conflicts (the "pessimistic" approach used by ordinary locking isolation levels), it optimistically assumes conflicts will be rare, lets everyone proceed without blocking, and only checks for an actual conflict at the very end, when a write is finally being committed.

**Why this happens in real databases.** The classic "read a row, think about it, then update it based on what you read" pattern — the same shape that causes the conversion deadlock covered elsewhere in this course — is just as relevant under SNAPSHOT isolation, but the danger here is different. Under SNAPSHOT, when you read a row, you're not locking it, and you're seeing a version of it frozen at the moment your transaction began — not necessarily the current, live version. If someone else changes that same row for real, and commits that change, while your transaction is still deciding what to do based on the older version it originally read, your eventual update is now based on stale information, and blindly proceeding with it could silently overwrite the other person's change as if it never happened.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** Under SNAPSHOT isolation, every row keeps a hidden version history in a special area called the version store (living in tempdb). When your transaction starts, it's effectively pinned to "the versions of every row as they existed at this moment" — any reads it does throughout the transaction see that frozen snapshot, regardless of what anyone else commits in the meantime. Now suppose your transaction reads a row from that snapshot, computes some new value based on what it read, and then tries to `UPDATE` that same row. Before actually committing that update, SQL Server checks: has this specific row been changed and committed by anyone else since my transaction's snapshot was taken? If yes — if some other session read-modified-and-committed a change to that exact row in the meantime — SQL Server refuses to let your update through blindly. Instead of silently overwriting a change your snapshot never even knew happened, it raises error 3960, an update-conflict error, and rolls back your transaction, forcing you to notice the conflict and decide what to do about it, rather than clobbering the other session's work without either side ever knowing.

**Why this matters in production.** Optimistic concurrency, of which SNAPSHOT isolation is SQL Server's built-in version, is a deliberate, popular trade-off in busy systems: it avoids the blocking and deadlocking headaches of traditional locking (readers and writers under SNAPSHOT genuinely don't block each other, unlike the default locking behavior covered in earlier lessons), at the cost of occasionally having to detect and reject a write that turned out to be based on stale data. Applications using SNAPSHOT isolation for exactly this reason need to actually handle error 3960 gracefully — typically by retrying the whole read-modify-write operation from scratch against fresh data — rather than treating it as an unexpected crash, because under real concurrent load on busy rows, this conflict is an expected, designed-for outcome, not a bug.

The fix demonstrated in this lesson takes one of two forms: either catch error 3960 in application code and retry the operation cleanly against fresh data (embracing the optimistic model as intended), or, if a particular operation is known in advance to be highly conflict-prone, avoid the optimistic gamble altogether for that specific case by taking an `UPDLOCK` on the initial read (much like the conversion-deadlock fix elsewhere in this course), which reserves the row pessimistically up front and serializes concurrent attempts cleanly, trading away some of SNAPSHOT's non-blocking benefit specifically where conflicts are likely enough that retrying constantly would itself become wasteful.

**Try it yourself.** The scenario below has two sessions read the same row under SNAPSHOT isolation and then both try to update it, and shows you the second session's commit failing with error 3960 the moment SQL Server detects the row changed since that session's snapshot was taken. Try retrying the failed operation against fresh data and watch it succeed cleanly the second time — a direct look at the retry pattern real applications need to build around optimistic concurrency, rather than treating error 3960 as an unexpected failure.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** SNAPSHOT isolation is a distinct setting from READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT (RCSI), even though both use row versioning under the hood — RCSI changes the behavior of the ordinary READ COMMITTED default (each individual statement sees the latest committed data at the moment it runs, with no update-conflict detection at all), while SNAPSHOT is an isolation level a transaction opts into explicitly, pinning the *entire transaction* to one consistent point in time and adding the update-conflict check covered in this lesson. It's worth being precise about which of the two a given system actually uses, since only true SNAPSHOT isolation raises error 3960 — RCSI never does, because it never promises a consistent whole-transaction snapshot in the first place.

## Scenario
A team moved a balance-transfer transaction to **`SNAPSHOT`** isolation to avoid blocking. Now, under load, transactions occasionally die outright with *"Snapshot isolation transaction aborted due to update conflict"* (**error 3960**) instead of waiting. Session A reads Alice's balance, and while it's thinking, Session B commits a change to that same row. When A finally updates, it is **rolled back**.

## Why it fails
`SNAPSHOT` is **optimistic**: at the start of the transaction A takes a consistent *version* of the data and never blocks readers or writers. But when A goes to `UPDATE` a row that **another committed transaction has changed since A's snapshot**, the engine can't reconcile the two — so instead of silently overwriting B's change, it aborts A with error 3960. Optimism assumes conflicts are rare; when they aren't, you get failures rather than waits.

## What to look for
- Session A ends in **error 3960** (update conflict), not a deadlock and not a block.
- B commits successfully in between A's read and A's write.

## The concept
SNAPSHOT is great for read-heavy, low-contention work, but a **read-modify-write** on a hot row needs to *reserve* that row. Either lower this transaction to the default **`READ COMMITTED`** (locking) so A's update simply serializes after B, or keep snapshot reads but take an **`UPDLOCK`** on the initial read so B can't slip in. The blunt operational answer is a retry loop — but preventing the conflict beats catching it.
startingQuery: -- This is a concurrency lesson. Change Session A so its read-then-update no longer aborts with error 3960, then Run the interleaving.
hints: A isn't blocked or deadlocked — it's aborted with error 3960 because the row it snapshotted was changed and committed by B before A's UPDATE.
Optimistic (SNAPSHOT) concurrency detects the conflict instead of waiting. To avoid it, A must either not use a stale snapshot or must reserve the row up front.
Drop A to READ COMMITTED so its UPDATE serializes after B (SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL READ COMMITTED), or add WITH (UPDLOCK) to A's initial SELECT.

interleaving.description: Session A reads Alice's row under SNAPSHOT; Session B updates and commits that row; A's later UPDATE aborts with error 3960 (update conflict).

A.sql: SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT; BEGIN TRAN; SELECT Balance FROM Accounts WHERE AccountId = 1;
UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 100 WHERE AccountId = 1; COMMIT;

B.sql: UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 50 WHERE AccountId = 1;

interleaving.solutionNote: A's read-then-write on a hot row can't use a stale optimistic snapshot. Either lower A to READ COMMITTED so its UPDATE serializes after B's committed change (no version conflict), or keep SNAPSHOT but add WITH (UPDLOCK) to A's initial SELECT so B cannot commit a change to the row first. Both make A complete instead of aborting with 3960.
